items.title: Student perceptions of generative artificial intelligence in university education: a study using the ZMET technique

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Introduction This study aims to analyse university students' perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in their academic education, exploring how they construct meaning around its use and how these representations influence notions of learning, authorship and critical literacy in higher education. Methods The sample comprised 20 students from Argentina, Chile, Mexico and Peru. The Zaltman Metaphor Elicitation Technique (ZMET) was employed as a qualitative elicitation approach using images and metaphorical narratives, applied via a two-phase protocol: a) a pre-task involving the independent selection of seven images; and b) a guided elicitation phase, based on questions that explore the participant's perception through analogies, sensory contrasts and emotional narratives. Results Within this corpus, participants articulated ambivalent representations of GenAI through several distinct metaphorical configurations, including an “other” to which participants attribute agency (a silent companion or tutor) and a pragmatic cognitive extension valued for its efficiency. These representations highlight a reconfiguration of the relationship between students and processes of knowledge production, blurring traditional boundaries between technological assistance, collaboration and authorship. On an emotional level, some accounts represented GenAI as an emotional buffer, offering relief from academic overload; however, this relief coexists with ethical vigilance and unease about “crossing a line” in academic honesty, reflecting processes of negotiation over intellectual responsibility and the legitimate use of generative systems in educational contexts. Discussion Regarding institutional adaptation, metaphors of misalignment and accounts of GenAI bridging gaps in academic support point to perceived gaps in institutional guidance and to the importance of pedagogical mediation, including clearer approaches to teaching and assessment in a context where GenAI is already part of university life. Taken together, the accounts show how participants interpret GenAI as a context-specific form of academic support and guidance. These representations link the negotiation of trust and authorship to the perceived accessibility of university support, offering insights into critical literacy and institutional mediation.

items.abstract_text: AI-generated visuals are increasingly being explored in higher education as tools to support student learning and reflection, yet little is known about how students experience their use in reflective assessment. This qualitative study explored the experiences and perceptions of first-year students ( n = 10) using AI-generated reflective visuals (AIGRVs) as part of a reflective assessment approach in a general education course at a Middle Eastern university. The study analyzed students' open-ended survey responses thematically to understand how they described and made sense of creating, interpreting, and evaluating AI-generated visuals as part of their learning. Basic quantitative results from the same surveys, including responses to Likert-scale statements, were also analysed and used as supplementary evidence to support the qualitative findings. The analysis highlighted four interconnected areas: engagement, conceptual understanding, critical reflection, and learning. Students described using AIGRVs to represent and connect course concepts, evaluate AI-generated outputs, and reflect on their learning experiences. The quantitative data were consistent with these accounts but were interpreted cautiously because of the very small samples. Overall, the study offers preliminary, context-specific insights into how AIGRVs may function as cognitive and metacognitive scaffolds within reflective assessment and identifies directions for larger and more rigorous studies.

items.title: Application of an AI-powered virtual simulation combined with case-based learning in undergraduate emergency medicine education: focusing on advanced clinical competence and clinical transfer ability

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background Emergency medicine is characterized by urgency, criticality, severity, and diversity, which places high demands on undergraduate medical education. Traditional lecture-based teaching has limitations in developing students' advanced clinical competence and clinical transfer ability. Although virtual simulation and case-based learning (CBL) have demonstrated benefits in medical education, their combined application in emergency medicine teaching has not been systematically evaluated, especially based on artificial intelligence (AI). This study primarily aimed to investigate whether the integrated AI-powered virtual simulation combined with CBL could improve students' higher-order clinical competencies and clinical transfer ability, and secondarily to obtain empirical evidence to support the optimization of undergraduate emergency medicine teaching. Methods Third-year undergraduate students majoring in clinical medicine were selected as the research subjects and randomly divided into the control group and the experimental group. The control group adopted the traditional teaching method, while the experimental group adopted the AI-enabled virtual simulation combined with real emergency case teaching method. The learning situation of the virtual simulation platform was automatically recorded by the platform, and the teaching effect was evaluated through theoretical scores, objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) scores, clinical practice tracking evaluation (including advanced clinical ability and clinical transfer effect evaluation), comprehensive evaluation of learning psychology, and teaching satisfaction questionnaire. Results Compared with the control group, the students in the experimental group demonstrated significant advantages in all assessment dimensions, including theoretical test, various practical skills in OSCE, disease assessment, emergency management, clinical decision-making, as well as learning confidence, autonomous learning ability and teaching satisfaction ( P &lt; 0.001). Further analysis indicated that within the experimental group, greater investment in study time was significantly associated with better clinical performance and diagnostic accuracy. Crucially, Cox regression analysis confirmed that diagnostic accuracy was an independent protective factor for the weakness of clinical transfer ability (HR = 0.6469, P &lt; 0.00001), meaning that students with higher diagnostic accuracy had a significantly superior clinical competence. Conclusions In conclusion, this study demonstrates that the teaching model combining AI-powered virtual simulation with real cases can comprehensively and significantly enhance the comprehensive clinical skills and learning experience of medical students. The teaching effect can effectively transfer to the real clinical environment, and the diagnostic accuracy cultivated during the teaching process has important predictive value for the long-term clinical prognosis. This provides empirical evidence for the reform of emergency medicine education and emphasizes the importance of linking educational process evaluation with clinical outcomes.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can support university learning, yet psychological reliance on AI-generated feedback may limit independent mastery experiences. Under an integrated I-PACE–social cognitive framework, this three-wave observational study examined whether self-efficacy for learning and performance statistically accounted for the association between AI dependence and subsequent academic engagement, and whether physical activity moderated the first-stage association. The analysis was based on 1,068 quality-screened students matched across baseline (T1), Week 4 (T2), and Week 8 (T3) questionnaires. AI dependence and physical activity were measured at T1, self-efficacy at T1/T2, and academic engagement at T1/T3. Standardized regression-based PROCESS Models 4 and 7 adjusted for baseline self-efficacy and engagement, demographics, and AI-use intensity. Higher T1 AI dependence was associated with lower T2 self-efficacy ( β = −0.137), while T2 self-efficacy was positively associated with T3 engagement ( β = 0.114). The first-stage interaction was small ( β = 0.073; ΔR 2 = 0.005), with an index of moderated mediation of 0.008 (5,000-resample 95% bootstrap CI [0.002, 0.017]). Inverse-probability-of-completion weighting produced similar core estimates; longitudinal measurement-invariance and latent autoregressive SEM results are additionally reported as sensitivity evidence. The results identify a short-term, temporally ordered indirect association involving academic self-efficacy, not an established causal mechanism. Educators may preserve students’ independent mastery opportunities when designing AI-assisted coursework.

items.abstract_text: Introduction Generative AI chatbots now give students instant commentary on their writing, yet little is known about how engaging with that commentary relates to the self-regulatory capacities on which writing development depends. This study examined a chain mediation model in which generative AI feedback use is associated with writing self-regulation through feedback literacy and, in turn, second language writing anxiety. Methods Non-English-major undergraduates at three universities in Henan Province, China, completed two surveys 12 weeks apart in the 2026 spring semester (wave 1 N = 650; 520 retained, 80.0%). Wave 1 assessed generative AI feedback use and feedback literacy; wave 2 assessed writing anxiety and writing self-regulation. Serial mediation analysis used 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples, with item-level validity checks and re-estimations without item parcels added as sensitivity analyses. Results Generative AI feedback use was positively associated with later writing self-regulation [ c = 0.265, 95% CI (0.190, 0.339)]. The total indirect effect was 0.128 [0.094, 0.167], or 48.3% of the total association: 0.086 [0.053, 0.122] via feedback literacy, 0.024 [0.008, 0.049] via writing anxiety, and 0.018 [0.009, 0.031] for the serial route. The direct association remained significant (c′ = 0.137). Focal paths kept their signs and significance when item parcels were removed and when only feedback-seeking items defined the predictor. Discussion These estimates describe associations rather than effects of an intervention. With no wave-1 baselines of anxiety or self-regulation and with two within-wave orderings resting on theory, the design cannot establish temporal sequence or within-person change. The pattern is consistent with a theoretically proposed ordering; the pedagogical suggestions are recommendations only, not demonstrated outcomes. The generative AI feedback use scale is a preliminary study-specific measure.

items.title: Beyond access: the evolution of Portugal’s pharmacy-based vaccination strategy and the future role of AI-driven outreach

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Vaccination programmes increasingly face a paradox: expanding access does not necessarily translate into coverage at policy targets. Portugal provides an instructive example. The integration of community pharmacies into seasonal influenza and COVID-19 vaccination created more than 3,500 vaccination points and approximately 70% of influenza doses were administered in pharmacies in 2023–2024. The pharmacy share then fell to under 46% by 2025–2026, while total influenza doses remained broadly stable (2.41 to 2.56 million per season). This indicates a redistribution of doses across settings rather than a loss of vaccination activity; changes in age eligibility, high-dose vaccination for adults aged ≥85 years in SNS units, and invitation and recall activity may all have contributed. Influenza coverage among adults aged ≥65 years remained below the World Health Organization target of 75%, at 70.5% in 2024–2025 and 73.0% in 2025–2026. This suggests that, residual under-vaccination reflects barriers beyond physical access. The authors use “activation gap” descriptively for potentially addressable interruptions between eligibility and vaccination. Portugal already uses registry-based invitations and reminders, the open question is what a conversational layer, scripted or based on generative AI, could add. Evidence is relatively strong for reminders, growing for scripted conversational interventions and preliminary for generative AI. The authors therefore propose a registry-based randomised comparison of existing recall, existing recall plus a scripted conversational intervention, and existing recall plus a generative-AI conversational intervention, with incremental vaccination, safety, equity, trust and cost per additional vaccinated person as outcomes.

items.abstract_text: Background As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) increasingly becomes a source of health information for patients, some patients and family members have already obtained relevant explanations or recommendations from AI and brought this information into clinical communication. This change may create new communication demands for nurses. This study aimed to explore clinical nurses’ communication experiences and response strategies when patients or family members introduced AI-generated health information into nurse–patient communication. Methods A qualitative descriptive design was adopted. Using purposive sampling combined with a maximum variation strategy, 18 clinical nurses with relevant communication experience were recruited from three tertiary hospitals in Sichuan Province and Shanghai, China. One-to-one semi-structured interviews were conducted between May and August 2026. The interviews focused on specific nurse–patient communication events personally experienced by the participants. Data were analyzed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis. Results Two themes and six subthemes were identified. The first theme, changes in nurse–patient communication in the context of AI, included seeking confirmation from or questioning nurses using AI-generated health information, increased explanatory work, and increased communication opportunities. The second theme, nurses’ responses to AI-generated health information, included identifying patients’ actual concerns, explaining information differences in relation to the patient’s specific situation, and maintaining communication while seeking professional support. Conclusion The introduction of AI-generated health information into nurse–patient communication may both increase nurses’ explanatory work and create new opportunities for communication. Nurses may need to consider patients’ existing understanding and actual concerns, explain discrepancies between AI-generated health information and clinical arrangements in relation to the patient’s specific situation, and seek professional support when necessary. These findings may inform efforts to support nurses’ communication skills, although their applicability across different clinical settings requires further exploration.

items.title: The limits of declarative authorship: the structural vulnerability of intellectual property in the age of generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative AI functions as a near zero cost execution engine, weakening the long standing reliance on human effort on which traditional intellectual property (IP) systems depend. The academic response has focused, so far, on studying productivity at the micro level, debating the doctrinal question of IP infringement through AI training at the macro level, or blunt denial of AI authorship. These responses miss the central problem: the human provenance at the heart of IP law is now cheap to falsify and hard to verify. In this paper I argue that AI output appropriation poses a significant threat to IP through an adverse selection dynamic. The threat comes from humans who use AI to appropriate its output and extract the value attached to human effort. Skill compression effects cutting across writing, coding, and consulting have begun to commoditize execution, compressing the quality distribution that once supported premium prices for IP protected output. This process is compounded by the difficulty of verifying declared human authorship or inventorship, which may reward deception and discourage honest effort. I therefore explore value migration from execution skill to concentrated complementary assets. Building on market evidence from platform economies, the paper considers an evolution of IP from a rights based asset model to a verification model, in which the human role shifts from creator to authenticator.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI can enable production without corresponding learning, yet wholesale exclusion from assessed work forgoes opportunities needed for workplace and lifelong learning. This article proposes learning-consequential assessment design. Students may use AI to produce assessed work, but success also depends on showing they possess the understanding their AI-supported work displays. Knowing this may encourage students to use AI for learning through explanation, comparison and challenge, rather than product optimisation alone. The central claim, that the understanding displayed is the learner's own, rests on coherence between their reasons for consequential decisions and their work, with independent performance corroborating where needed. Evidence may also warrant three capability claims: learner-directed production with AI, accountable verification of AI-shaped work and independent capability. Learning Orchestration describes the cognitive-metacognitive, epistemic and ethical judgement through which learners coordinate AI and other resources for learning, production and verification; teacher orchestration describes how teaching and assessment support its development.

items.abstract_text: This study examined how internal control systems and ethical oversight shape corporate governance effectiveness in AI-driven organisations, using listed deposit money banks in Nigeria as the focus. The increasing use of artificial intelligence in banking operations has introduced governance risks that traditional control systems may no longer fully address. Previous studies mostly considered internal controls, ethics, and governance as separate issues, with limited evidence on how they work together in emerging economies. The study therefore assessed the effects of Risk Assessment, Control Activities, Information and Communication, and Monitoring Activities on Tobin’s Q, and also examined the moderating role of Ethical Oversight. A correlational and panel data research design was adopted. Secondary data were sourced from the audited annual reports and accounts of 13 listed deposit money banks in Nigeria for the period 2015 to 2024. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, Hausman specification test, and random effects regression were used for the analysis. The findings showed that all the internal control variables had positive and significant effects on Tobin’s Q, while Information and Communication had the strongest influence. Ethical Oversight also showed a positive direct effect and significantly strengthened the relationship between internal control systems and firm value. The study concludes that effective internal controls, when supported by credible ethical governance, improve market performance and broaden the traditional view of corporate governance in technology-driven institutions. It therefore recommends that deposit money banks strengthen risk management systems, widen internal audits to cover AI systems, establish active ethics committees, invest in secure digital reporting platforms, and provide continuous governance training for directors and compliance officers.

items.abstract_text: Purpose: This study synthesizes research on Responsible AI in education to develop an Islamic ethical framework that supports human agency, cognitive autonomy, and academic integrity. Method: We conducted a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) using PRISMA 2020 and analyzed 50 articles published between 2022 and 2026 from Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, Dimensions, and Google Scholar. Findings: Research has shifted from technology acceptance toward ethics and governance, although it remains dominated by higher education and cross-sectional designs. Responsible AI principles include transparency, accountability, fairness, and human oversight. The Islamic perspective strengthens these principles through maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah and the values of amanah, 'adl, ihsan, sidq, and tabayyun. The relationship between AI and human agency, cognitive autonomy, and academic integrity is conditional: reflective and verified use tends to support these dimensions, whereas dependence may undermine them. Novelty: This review's findings point to a shift from governance-centered responsibility to moral-epistemic responsibility, with three propositions: tabayyun as an obligation of epistemic verification, hifẓ al-‘aql as an educational orientation, and integrating AI governance with moral-educational development. Contribution: This study provides a conceptual foundation for responsible AI use in Islamic education by placing human oversight, information verification, independent thinking, and academic integrity at its core. Future Research: Future studies should test these propositions through longitudinal and experimental designs and develop instruments that integrate Islamic ethical values, human agency, cognitive autonomy, and academic integrity. Tujuan: Kajian ini bertujuan mensintesis penelitian mengenai Responsible AI dalam pendidikan untuk merumuskan kerangka etika Islam yang mendukung agensi manusia, otonomi kognitif, dan integritas akademik. Metode: Systematic Literature Review (SLR) berdasarkan PRISMA 2020 dengan menganalisis 50 artikel terbitan 2022–2026 dari Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, Dimensions, dan Google Scholar. Temuan: Penelitian bergeser dari penerimaan teknologi menuju etika dan tata kelola, meskipun masih didominasi oleh pendidikan tinggi dan desain cross-sectional. Prinsip Responsible AI meliputi transparansi, akuntabilitas, keadilan, dan pengawasan manusia. Perspektif Islam memperkuatnya melalui maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah serta nilai amanah, 'adl, ihsan, sidq, dan tabayyun. Hubungan AI dengan agensi manusia, otonomi kognitif, dan integritas akademik bersifat kondisional: penggunaan reflektif dan terverifikasi cenderung mendukung, sedangkan ketergantungan berisiko melemahkan. Kebaruan: Temuan kajian ini mengarah pada pergeseran dari governance-centered responsibility menuju moral-epistemic responsibility, dengan tiga proposisi: tabayyun sebagai kewajiban verifikasi epistemik, hifẓ al-‘aql sebagai orientasi pendidikan, serta integrasi tata kelola AI dan pembentukan moral-edukatif. Kontribusi: Memberikan dasar konseptual penggunaan AI yang bertanggung jawab dalam pendidikan Islam dengan menempatkan pengawasan manusia, verifikasi informasi, kemandirian berpikir, dan integritas akademik sebagai inti. Penelitian Selanjutnya: Menguji proposisi melalui desain longitudinal, eksperimental, dan pengembangan instrumen yang mengintegrasikan nilai etika Islam, agensi manusia, otonomi kognitif, dan integritas akademik.

items.title: Explainable AI (XAI) for Convolutional Neural Networks in Early Cancer Detection

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
items.abstract_text: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become useful tools for analysing medical images because they can learn visual patterns associated with normal and abnormal tissue. In cancer screening and diagnosis, however, a high classification score alone is not sufficient: clinicians also need to understand which image regions influenced a model’s output. This paper proposes an explainable deep-learning framework that combines CNN-based image classification with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods to support early cancer detection from histopathological images. The proposed workflow includes image collection, quality assessment, preprocessing, augmentation, CNN training, prediction, and explanation generation. Grad-CAM is used to produce class-specific heatmaps, while LIME and SHAP are considered for local image-region and feature-contribution explanations. The explanations are intended to help users inspect whether the model focuses on tissue regions that are relevant to the predicted class rather than irrelevant background patterns. Model performance can be assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, specificity, and area under the ROC curve. Explanation quality should additionally be examined through localization agreement, stability, and review by qualified domain experts. The framework is presented as a research proposal; its diagnostic performance and clinical usefulness must be established through controlled experiments and external validation. It is designed as a decision-support approach and is not intended to replace professional diagnosis.

items.title: Multimodal artificial intelligence and large language models in gastrointestinal endoscopy: From lesion detection to workflow-integrated report generation

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, with most early applications focusing on computer-aided detection and diagnosis of lesions from endoscopic images. However, real-world endoscopic practice extends beyond image interpretation. Endoscopists must integrate real-time video, anatomical location, lesion morphology, procedural context, histopathological findings, clinical history, and standardized terminology to make diagnostic decisions and generate clinically meaningful reports. Recent advances in multimodal AI and large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to move beyond isolated endoscopic image analysis toward more comprehensive endoscopic workflow support. By integrating visual, textual, temporal, and clinical information, these models can support lesion characterization, anatomical navigation, procedure quality assessment, structured documentation, report generation, and patient-centered communication. Nevertheless, clinical translation remains limited by scarce high-quality multimodal datasets, heterogeneous reporting standards, insufficient external validation, hallucination risk, limited interpretability, real-time integration challenges, privacy concerns, and evolving regulation. This review summarizes current applications of AI in GI endoscopy, with particular emphasis on the emerging role of multimodal learning and LLMs in bridging lesion detection, context-aware interpretation, and automated report generation. Furthermore, the article analyzes future challenges and the methodological, clinical, ethical, and regulatory requirements for the reliable integration of these systems into clinical endoscopic practice.

items.title: Coping with sustainability information overload:  The role of generative artificial intelligence literacy

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Ho Chi Minh City Open University Journal of Science - Economics and Business Administration
items.abstract_text: Consumers can use sustainability information to consume responsibly; however, excessive and complex sustainability claims might confuse consumers and hinder proper evaluations. Based on cognitive appraisal theory, this study empirically investigates the impacts of sustainability information overload (SIO) on green information avoidance (GIA) and green information verification behavior (GIVB) and examines the moderating role of generative AI literacy (GAIL) and the associations of GIA and GIVB with green purchase decision confidence (GPDC). Data from an online cross-sectional survey of 468 adult consumers in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings revealed that SIO positively influenced GIA, and GIA negatively influenced GPDC. However, SIO did not negatively influence GIVB on average. GAIL significantly moderated the SIO-GIVB relationship: SIO was negatively associated with GIVB at low GAIL but not significantly at mean or high GAIL.GIVB positively influenced GPDC. An indirect effect of SIO on GPDC through GIA is significant, but the indirect effect through GIVB is not significant unconditionally. These results suggest that sustainability information overload is associated with distinct coping responses. From a practical perspective, sustainability portals and shopping applications involving GenAI should emphasize evaluability and verifiability rather than enhancing disclosures. Through defining GAIL as a digitally mediated capability from the consumer’s perspective which can serve as a coping tool, this paper builds on cognitive appraisal theory in the context of AI-mediated sustainable consumption and explains the critical engagement of consumers with sustainability information amid overload situations.

items.title: <b>Roles and Research Focus of AI in Mathematics Education: Insights from a Systematic Literature Review and Bibliometric Analysis</b>

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology
items.abstract_text: In this study, we adopted a holistic approach by integrating bibliometric analysis and systematic review methods to thoroughly evaluate the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics education and its research trends. The study aims to understand the current state of the field and provide strategic direction for future research by assessing general trends, intellectual contributions, and application potential in AI-focused mathematics education research from a multidimensional perspective. In the first phase, we conducted a content analysis of 363 articles published in high-quality journals indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database, focusing on dimensions such as publishers, method types, research designs, study groups, theoretical or conceptual frameworks, data collection techniques, preferred technologies, purposes of use, and roles. Subsequently, we conducted a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of scientific productivity, citation performance, collaboration networks, conceptual structures, thematic maps, and intellectual transformations. During this process, we followed the guidelines outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA). The findings indicate that AI technologies have been increasingly utilized in mathematics education, with significant growth observed since 2015. AI-focused mathematics education research has been predominantly concentrated in countries like the USA, China, and Germany, delving into areas such as personalized learning, assessment, feedback, and pedagogical innovations. Most studies have employed quantitative and mixed methods, with middle school and undergraduate students being the primary target groups. Bibliometric analyses reveal a rapid expansion in scientific productivity and collaboration networks, while thematic trends primarily focus on personalized learning and the integration of digital tools.

items.title: <b>AI as a New Problem Generator in the Context of Mathematical Modelling</b>

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology
items.abstract_text: Having been studied for centuries, mathematical modelling is an important perspective in mathematics education; however, teachers often face difficulties in accessing appropriate and high-quality modelling activities for classroom use. This study investigates the capacity of ChatGPT and its customised version, the Mathematical Modelling Problem Generator (MMPG), to produce mathematically and pedagogically meaningful modelling problems. Four AI-generated model-eliciting activities were comparatively analysed: three produced in independent ChatGPT-4 sessions and one produced by MMPG, all focusing on ratios and proportions. The problem scenarios were evaluated using five characteristics from established frameworks, focusing on context (non-routine and real-life relevance) and complexity (multiple steps, uncertain solution paths, and multiple solutions). The results show that ChatGPT failed to produce MEAs that met key modelling characteristics, whereas MMPG successfully generated non-routine, multi-step MEAs with unclear solution paths and multiple valid solutions. Therefore, MMPG can be considered an effective tool for supporting pedagogical practice by improving teachers’ access to and design of content-aligned, high-quality modelling activities.

items.title: Studyflow: Evidence-Informed Design and Prototyping of an AI-Assisted Academic Workload and Cognitive Support Platform for University Students Aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: University students, particularly those who also work or hold organizational roles, frequently experience academic overload, stress, and burnout. Existing digital tools tend to address either task management or well-being, rarely both, and many lose users within days. This study reports the evidence-informed design of StudyFlow, a mobile-first platform that helps students turn unstructured academic demands into a prioritized, actionable plan, and examines how its design aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A design science research approach was followed. A targeted narrative review of literature published from 2021 to 2026 on student stress, working students, digital well-being interventions, engagement, and gamification informed a proto-persona, eight use cases, and nine functional requirements. A high-fidelity interactive prototype was generated through a five-stage natural-language prompt sequence in Google Stitch and refined in Google AI Studio. The intended feature set was compared with four widely used productivity and well-being applications, and each feature group was mapped to SDG targets with measurable evaluation indicators. The review yielded seven design implications, each traced to specific requirements and interface decisions. The prototype implements a four-stage workflow (set up, capture, organize and act, reflect) across dashboard, brain dump, task, focus, insights, and settings screens. None of the four comparator applications supported academic assignment breakdown, and none combined task capture, prioritization, focus support, reflection, and progress feedback in a single workflow. Streaks and usage metrics were deliberately framed as optional, non-punitive cues. StudyFlow shows how evidence on student stress and app engagement can be translated into a coherent, low-friction design that targets student well-being (SDG Target 3.4), persistence in tertiary education (Target 4.3), and the inclusion of working students (Target 10.2). Because no user testing has yet been conducted, no effectiveness claims are made; a staged usability and pilot evaluation protocol is proposed.

items.title: Generative Ai-Enabled Financial Forecasting and Strategic Financial Decision Quality in Emerging-Market SMEs

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal of Economics, Finance And Management Studies
items.abstract_text: This study investigates how generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and business analytics capability shape strategic financial decision quality in emerging market SMEs, with particular attention to the moderating role of AI governance maturity. Grounded in organizational information processing theory and dynamic capabilities theory, the study argues that better financial decisions depend not simply on access to advanced technologies, but on how effectively firms turn AI generated forecasts and analytical information into useful financial judgment. AI governance maturity is expected to strengthen this process by providing appropriate oversight, accountability, validation, and control over the use of AI generated financial information. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted with 385 respondents who possessed relevant knowledge of SME financial management, business analytics, AI applications, or organizational decision making. Data were collected using a five-point Likert scale questionnaire and analyzed with IBM SPSS version 26. Reliability analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and multiple linear regression were performed, while Hayes’ Process Macro Model 1 was used to test the moderating effect. The results show that generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability (β = 0.613) and business analytics capability (β = 0.487) both have significant positive effects on strategic financial decision quality. AI governance maturity also strengthens the relationship between generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and strategic financial decision quality, with an interaction coefficient of 0.518. These findings suggest that emerging market SMEs gain greater value from generative AI when forecasting tools are supported by sound analytical capabilities and governance practices. Effective financial decision making therefore requires not only better technology, but also the organizational capacity to interpret, review, and responsibly use AI generated financial insights.

items.title: Fact-Checking: A Survey on Content Verification in the Age of AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: In a global information environment characterised by strong propaganda pressures and a lack of transparency, the demand for independent, high-quality sources is constantly growing. A significant gap is thus emerging between the growing complexity of information flows and users' ability to critically evaluate information. Currently, neither information professionals nor engaged citizens are able to accurately verify every single piece of news, nor do they have access to online platforms capable of selecting, verifying, and aggregating thematic content based on shared quality criteria. The lack of human and technical resources severely hinders the creation of information ecosystems resilient to disinformation. To address this challenge, recent efforts have focused on integrated platforms that combine human expertise with advanced automated analysis tools. Technologies such as machine learning, semantic analysis, and generative artificial intelligence offer innovative solutions for processing large volumes of data and supporting automated fact-checking. Nonetheless, the evolution of these technologies introduces new complexities, reshaping content production and distribution. Algorithms often amplify information polarisation. Traditional media increasingly align with partisan political and economic interests, losing credibility. As a result, citizens align themselves with different news sources in an attempt to reconstruct the truth within a fragmented digital landscape. By bringing together the analysis of manipulative strategies, the evolution of verification methods, hybrid human–AI workflows, and the requirements of explainability within a single survey, the article aims to offer researchers and practitioners a more integrated reference point for the design of effective and accountable verification systems.

items.title: EXPLORING THE INFLUENCE OF CHATGPT ON ESL WRITING BEHAVIOURS: A CASE  STUDY IN A MALAYSIAN SECONDARY SCHOOL

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: This qualitative case study examined how ten secondary school ESL students in Malaysia used ChatGPT when revising their writing. The study did not focus on writing scores. Instead, it looked at students’ writing behaviours, the decisions they made when using ChatGPT, and the changes that appeared between their first and revised drafts. The students first wrote an essay on “Having a Balanced Diet” without using ChatGPT. After a short introduction to the tool, students revised the same essay with the help of ChatGPT. Data collection took place through writing samples from the students and semi-structured interviews. The interview data were analysed using thematic analysis, while the comparison between the first and the second drafts was conducted using document analysis. From the findings, it is clear that the students made use of ChatGPT to go through grammar, vocabulary, sentence structure, and content of their essays. Many improvements had been made in the revised drafts. Most of the students managed to fix grammar errors and use more suitable vocabulary, along with presenting new ideas in their work. Nonetheless, there are some flaws in the second drafts such as incorrect expressions, informal language and some incorrect ideas. The interviews also showed that the students did not accept the suggestions directly. The students chose those suggestions which were clear to them, appropriate to the task and related to their original meaning. Overall, the study shows that ChatGPT may be used to support ESL writing revision but students still need teacher guidance and their own judgement to use it critically and responsibly.

items.title: Emotionally Aware AI Chatbots for Adolescents: A Review of Psychological Principles for Learning, Calibrated Trust, and Healthy Human–AI Interaction

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal of Education, Humanities and Social Sciences
items.abstract_text: Conversational artificial intelligence now belongs to ordinary adolescent life, but the psychological research that should guide its design spreads over fields which seldom cite each other. Research on adolescent development, on misinformation susceptibility, on trust in automation, on chatbot-supported learning and on companion-chatbot overreliance has grown up separately, and each of these areas answers only part of the question of how a general-purpose chatbot should talk to a teenager. This paper brings together twenty-one sources from developmental psychology, human factors, human-computer interaction and educational technology, in order to show what is now known about adolescent chatbot interaction and what this means for conversational design. Three results appear repeatedly in this research. First, adolescence is a design context of its own, not a smaller version of adulthood, since reward sensitivity, social influence and emotional regulation are still developing, while exposure to persuasive conversational systems has already reached almost everyone. Second, trust in a chatbot changes behavior in ways that can be measured; thus, the proper design target is calibrated trust rather than maximal trust. Third, the failure modes that matter most for adolescent users, that is, hallucination, sycophancy and unwarranted confidence, originate in the model; the user is not their source. From these results this paper consolidates ten conversational design principles into four clusters, namely epistemic calibration, metacognitive scaffolding, bounded emotional support and autonomy preservation. The framework here is a conceptual synthesis and puts forward testable predictions, but it has not been empirically validated.

items.title: Bounded AI Assistance in Higher Education: Re-Aligning Pedagogy, Assessment and Institutional Governance

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has led universities and other higher education institutions to rethink the ways in which knowledge is conveyed, learning is facilitated, and academic performance is evaluated. While such technologies present possibilities for tailored explanations, feedback that supports learning as it unfolds, and joint inquiry, they also give rise to concerns regarding inaccurate information, reliance on machines for thinking, academic integrity, and inequities in access. Drawing on a narrative synthesis of selected literature and institutional guidance, this conceptual paper explores the pedagogical ramifications of LLMs. The paper contends that integrating them effectively demands learning and research environments that bring together subject-specific knowledge, critical questioning, openness about bounded AI use, and demonstrable competence. Constructive alignment, self-regulated learning, cognitive load theory, and cognitive engagement supply the conceptual bases for linking intended learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities, and assessment. A cyclical process is put forward, comprising independent engagement, AI-assisted interaction under guidance, verification, application, and reflection. The paper goes on to elaborate dimensions of institutional policy, encompassing governance, curriculum, assessment, research integrity, privacy, intellectual property, equity, procurement, and quality assurance. Specific consideration is devoted to contexts with constrained ICT resources. The paper's conclusion is that the educational value of LLMs rests on purposeful design of specific institutional AI policy that is clear, transparent and progressive.

items.title: AI-Enabled Digital Twins for Predictive Maintenance: A Case Study

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Scientific Journal of Engineering and Management
items.abstract_text: The increasing use of automation and advanced machinery in modern industries has made equipment reliability and operational efficiency important factors in industrial production. Unexpected machine failures can interrupt production activities, increase maintenance expenses, and affect overall productivity. Traditional maintenance approaches, such as reactive and preventive maintenance, are often unable to identify early signs of equipment failure or accurately determine when maintenance is actually required. To overcome these limitations, this paper explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Twin technology for predictive maintenance in industrial environments. A Digital Twin is a virtual representation of a physical machine or industrial system that is continuously updated using data collected from sensors installed on the actual equipment. By combining this technology with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning algorithms, it becomes possible to monitor equipment conditions, analyse operational patterns, detect abnormal behaviour, and predict potential failures before they cause major interruptions. The proposed approach integrates Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, real-time data acquisition, data preprocessing, virtual equipment modelling, and AI-based predictive analysis into a unified maintenance framework. Machine learning techniques such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks can be applied for fault detection, condition monitoring, and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation. This paper presents a case-study-based investigation of AI-enabled Digital Twins for industrial equipment monitoring, with particular emphasis on understanding how real-time data and predictive analytics can improve maintenance planning. It also examines the system architecture, working methodology, potential advantages, implementation challenges, and limitations of the proposed approach. The study highlights the potential of integrating AI with Digital Twin technology to transform conventional maintenance practices into more intelligent, data-driven, and condition-based systems, thereby supporting improved equipment reliability, reduced unplanned downtime, and more efficient industrial operations. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Digital Twin, Predictive Maintenance, Machine Learning, Internet of Things (IoT), Industry 4.0, Fault Detection, Condition Monitoring, Remaining Useful Life (RUL).

items.title: Generative AI adoption in organizations: A conceptual model of job crafting, employee productivity, creativity and work engagement

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Business and Management (IJBM)
items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping organizational work, yet its behavioural consequences for employees remain unevenly understood. Existing research on productivity, creativity and engagement is fragmented and rarely examined within a single theoretical framework. Drawing on Job Demands Resources theory, Conservation of Resources theory and Self Determination Theory, this conceptual paper develops an integrative model of how organizational GenAI adoption affects employee productivity, creativity and work engagement. Job crafting is proposed as the central behavioural mechanism. The model treats GenAI as both a job resource and a job demand. It therefore recognizes a double edged pathway in which technology insecurity and passive over reliance can offset the benefits of adoption. AI literacy, ethical use clarity and organizational readiness are identified as boundary conditions that determine which pathway prevails. Four hypotheses are developed, covering the mediating role of job crafting for productivity and engagement, its moderating role for creativity, and the conditioning effect of AI literacy and ethical guidance. A time lagged, multi source survey design, supplemented by supervisor ratings and an optional field experiment, is proposed for future empirical testing. The paper offers a resource based account of human and AI collaboration. It also provides managerial guidance for organizations that want GenAI adoption to deliver sustainable gains in performance and well being rather than short lived efficiency gains that erode over time.

items.title: The Cognitive Offloading Dilemma: Exploring How Generative AI Dependency Shapes Students’ Independent Thinking, Cognitive Confidence, and Intellectual Autonomy

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: A polished assignment can conceal who chose the method, weighed the evidence and reached the conclusion, which makes a student’s independent reasoning difficult to assess. Drawing on the metacognitive account of cognitive offloading and Social Cognitive Theory, this qualitative study examined how reliance on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) relates to independent thinking, cognitive confidence and intellectual autonomy. Semi-structured online interviews were conducted with 22 undergraduate and postgraduate students, aged 20 to 29, from universities in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, Pakistan, each describing a recent academic episode involving GenAI. Thematic analysis traced when students sought assistance, which decisions they delegated and how they later justified their choices, and produced six themes. Delegating study planning preserved autonomy when students kept control over content, whereas removing a familiar AI prompt exposed difficulty in selecting a method despite earlier success with calculations. Confidence also diverged from accuracy: one student withheld a sound answer without AI confirmation, while another trusted a diagnosis because AI agreed with it, although both had missed the same error. Comparing drafts, checking sources and answering peers’ questions helped students identify assumptions and give reasons for revision. The findings support assessment practices that distinguish producing an answer with assistance from being able to explain or defend it without assistance.

items.abstract_text: The rapid expansion of global e-commerce has intensified competition for consumer attention, rendering traditional demographic-segmented and rule-based marketing increasingly ineffective. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative paradigm in digital marketing, enabling firms to process high-velocity behavioral datasets and deliver hyper-personalized customer journeys in real time. While industry adoption of AI marketing tools is widespread, a substantial maturity gap persists between experimental deployment and fully scaled conversion optimization. This paper integrates a multi-stage analytical research design—combining psychometric Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) of consumer survey data ($N = 420$), econometric before-and-after funnel cohort modeling across retail deployments, and regression-based moderation analysis—to quantify how AI-enabled digital marketing drives sales conversion. Specifically, the study examines four core strategic pillars: neural recommendation engines, predictive programmatic acquisition, dynamic pricing optimization, and generative conversational AI. Analytical results demonstrate that Perceived Personalization significantly enhances Customer Experience Quality ($\beta = 0.499, p < 0.001$) and Digital Marketing Effectiveness ($\beta = 0.488, p < 0.001$), which jointly mediate downstream Purchase Intention and actual checkout conversion ($R^2 = 0.412$). Econometric cohort tracking further reveals a 23.4% to 31.0% relative lift in session-to-purchase conversion rates, a 27% reduction in bounce rates, and up to a 50% increase in Average Order Value (AOV) via real-time affinity bundling. However, moderation analysis confirms that perceived algorithmic opacity and privacy intrusion negatively attenuate conversion gains ($\beta = -0.214, p < 0.01$). The study concludes with an actionable governance and MLOps framework for balancing algorithmic conversion efficiency with consumer trust.

items.venue: OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development
items.abstract_text: Abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into workplaces is transforming not only how employees perform their tasks but also how they experience work. However, the implications of this transformation for sustainable development remain insufficiently understood, particularly regarding whether AI-enabled workplaces can support employees’ long-term well-being and resilience. Addressing this gap, this study examines how positive attitudes toward Generative AI (POS_ATT) and responsible AI signals (RAIS) contribute to multidimensional Green Well-being through employee engagement (ENG). Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, Signaling Theory, and the Job Demands–Resources theory, Green Well-being is conceptualized as a sustainable state encompassing emotional (GEW), cognitive (GCW), and social well-being (GSW). A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 342 knowledge workers employed by Vietnamese organizations using Generative AI. Participants were recruited using convenience and snowball sampling. The proposed model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The results show that both POS_ATT (β = 0.312, p < 0.001) and RAIS (β = 0.287, p < 0.001) are positively associated with employee engagement. ENG, in turn, is positively associated with all three dimensions of Green Well-being, with the strongest relationship observed for emotional well-being (β = 0.441), followed by cognitive (β = 0.418) and social well-being (β = 0.397), all at p < 0.001. Moreover, ENG fully mediates the relationships between POS_ATT and RAIS and the three Green Well-being dimensions. These findings broaden understanding of sustainable development in AI-enabled workplaces by showing that the potential human benefits of Generative AI are not associated solely with technology adoption. Rather, favorable employee perceptions and responsible implementation need to be translated into meaningful work engagement before they are associated with sustainable well-being outcomes. The study therefore identifies responsible AI, employee engagement, and multidimensional well-being as interconnected elements of a human-centered approach to sustainable digital transformation. Practically, organizations should complement investments in AI capabilities with transparent, explainable, and fair AI governance and engagement-oriented work design to preserve and develop human resources during digital transformation. Because the cross-sectional design captures relationships at a single point in time, the findings establish associations rather than causal effects. Longitudinal and cross-national research is therefore needed to examine whether these relationships persist over time and contribute to long-term employee and organizational resilience. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence; responsible AI; employee engagement; Green Well-being; sustainable development; sustainable digital transformation.

items.abstract_text: Parsons problems have been widely recognised to support novice learners by reducing the cognitive demands of writing code from scratch through rearrangement of provided code blocks. A common variation includes distractors – erroneous blocks of code which do not belong to the correct solution. While Parsons problems have been widely studied for introductory programming, they remain underexplored in various domains including in data science education, where students may possess statistical knowledge but limited programming experience. Developing distractors is also time-consuming for educators. This study investigated the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to generate semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems. A set of distractors was generated for 315 Python-based data science Parsons problems and was evaluated for pedagogical plausibility, compilability, and output divergence. Validated distractors were then incorporated as exemplars in a refined prompt to generate a second set of distractors, which were evaluated using the same criteria. The findings demonstrate that LLMs can be used to develop semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems and refining the prompts using validated exemplars further improved the quality. This study contributes to the limited literature on data science Parsons problems, distractor design and LLM-supported development of these problems.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI is increasingly used in learning environments, yet sustained interaction does not necessarily indicate cognitively engaged learning. This exploratory study examined how conversation openings related to cognitive engagement levels and the support orientations reflected in student messages during student-AI interactions. Cognitive engagement was classified by an adapted ICAP framework, openings were organised into a descriptive typology, and semantic thematic analysis was conducted on student messages. Openings oriented towards strategy guidance, conceptual explanation, error understanding, and resource review feedback were more often associated with moderate or deep engagement, whereas resource-evaluation openings were often associated with longer interactions despite limited cognitive depth. items.abstract_text: In spite of the fact that there is widespread agreement regarding the ethical principles that need to guide artificial intelligence, there is still a significant gap between these normative objectives and the operational realities of technical implementation. An investigation into how to operationalize a proactive, iterative AI governance paradigm is the focus of this study. The investigation is conducted via the prism of private law liabilities and constant technical verification. Both corporate compliance theater and opportunistic ethics shopping are the driving forces behind our inquiry. Both of these shortcomings in practice have occurred repeatedly. During the course of the study, a multi-layered methodological framework is utilized. This framework triangulates a comparative assessment of growing international regulatory frameworks and a "cross-sectoral typological mapping of auditing procedures from banking, data privacy, and environmental law." The findings reveal a systemic disconnect: corporate ethical commitments continue to be largely detached from operational audit systems, leaving data scientists frustrated by guidelines that are too abstract to act on. Furthermore, existing environmental, social, and governance standards do not provide any AI-specific tools for quantifying the hidden socio-technical harms that are embedded in global supply chains. rules that are abstract, whereas the existing ESG standards do not provide the AI-specific guidance that is required to assess the hidden socio-technical damages that are present throughout global supply chains.The purpose of this article is to offer a solution to this problem by advocating for the transition from voluntary soft law to an enforceable, longitudinal regulatory framework. We propose that corporate governance frameworks be merged with automated auditing pipelines, value-based engineering (also known as ethics-by-design), and independent third-party oversight. This would result in the transformation of abstract ethical concepts into private law duties that can be verified.

items.venue: International Journal of Sports Science and Human Performance
items.abstract_text: Background: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) show frequent motor difficulties, lower physical activity (PA) and fewer opportunities for sport participation than their peers. Individualized programs are therefore needed. Artificial intelligence (AI), wearable sensors and the Internet of Things (IoT) could support such personalization, but the evidence base has not been examined from a sport-science perspective. Objective: To synthesize evidence on PA interventions and AI- and IoT-enabled technologies relevant to children with ASD and to propose a framework for personalized, AI-supported sport and PA programs. Methods: A narrative review, guided by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA), combined a previously completed thematic synthesis of 49 studies of AI- and IoT-enabled assistive systems for children with disabilities (16 ASD-related) with targeted searches of PubMed/MEDLINE and publisher databases up to November 2026. Results: Meta-analyses indicate moderate benefits of PA interventions for motor skills, skill-related fitness and social functioning (e.g., Hedges' g = 0.62), although study quality is generally low. ASD-focused AI research mainly addresses gesture recognition, emotion analysis and socially assistive robotics in small samples (about 10–24 children), and none has tested fitness outcomes. The proposed artificial intelligence of things (AIoT)-CARE framework (Capability, Applicability, Robustness, and Ethics and Safety) links five stages: co-designed profiling, an accessible activity catalog, consent-based sensing, explainable recommendations with human override, and family-involved review. Conclusion: AI-supported personalization is a promising design direction, not a proven intervention. Phased evaluation using participant-level validation, real-world testing and AI-specific reporting guidelines is required.

items.abstract_text: With AI’s increasing role in digital marketing, a brand’s transparency about its use of AI could act as an informational signal of accountability. However, the interpretation consumers make of such transparency might vary with their knowledge of AI and their perception of persuasive intent. This study examines the relationship between perceived AI marketing transparency, brand trust, and purchase intention and the role of perceived manipulative intent as a mechanism and AI literacy as a boundary condition. We surveyed 387 matched Pakistani consumers, in two waves. AI literacy was operationalised with the core 18-item AI literacy dimensions of the MAILS instrument (use and apply AI, know and understand AI, detect AI, and AI ethics), whereas the remaining MAILS dimensions were treated as separate constructs. We tested the hypotheses using regression-based simple mediation (PROCESS Model 4) and first-stage moderated mediation (PROCESS Model 7). Perceived AI marketing transparency was positively associated with brand trust (β = 0.24, p < 0.001). Brand trust carried a significant indirect association between perceived AI marketing transparency and purchase intention (indirect effect = 0.06, 95% CI [0.02, 0.11]); the direct association was not statistically significant (c′ = 0.10, p = 0.081). Perceived manipulative intent was negatively associated with brand trust (b = −0.25, p < 0.001). AI literacy positively moderated the association between perceived AI marketing transparency and perceived manipulative intent (B = 0.13, p = 0.031), such that this association was positive and significant only at high AI literacy (B = 0.25, p < 0.001). The conditional indirect association was statistically distinguishable from zero only at high AI literacy (effect = −0.06, 95% CI [−0.13, −0.01]). The index of moderated mediation was statistically significant at the 5% level (index = −0.03, 95% CI [−0.07, −0.001]) but the CI was close to the null value. The results are consistent with both theoretically opposite mechanisms suggested: an accountability-related association between perceived transparency and brand trust, and a conditional suspicion-related indirect association via perceived manipulative intent, which were analysed under the umbrella of two different empirical models. The interaction was small and the moderated-mediation evidence was statistically weak and should be considered a preliminary rather than a general finding of the negative effects on transparency. One of the contributions of the study is distinguishing perceived transparency from its interpretation, and examining core AI literacy competencies in addition to a focused measure of persuasion knowledge activation in the context of AI marketing and signaling research. Finally, practical implications highlight the importance of AI disclosure being credible and context-specific, not necessarily a strategy that builds trust.

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has transformed learning practices, raising critical concerns regarding its influence on cognitive engagement, analytical reasoning, and knowledge retention. This study experimentally examines whether GenAI-assisted learning reduces cognitive load at the expense of deep thinking and sustained knowledge acquisition. A randomized controlled experimental design was employed involving 120 undergraduate students, randomly assigned to an experimental group utilizing ChatGPT (n = 60) and a control group completing equivalent learning activities without AI assistance (n = 60). Participants undertook analytical reading, conceptual problem-solving, and critical reasoning tasks under standardized experimental conditions. Cognitive load was measured using a mental effort rating scale, deep thinking was assessed through rubric-based analytical reasoning evaluations, and knowledge retention was examined using immediate and delayed post-tests administered two weeks apart. Results revealed significantly lower perceived cognitive load among AI-assisted learners (M = 3.42, SD = 1.11) compared with the control group (M = 5.76, SD = 1.24), t(118) = 10.88, p < .001. Conversely, students learning without AI demonstrated superior deep-thinking performance (M = 78.40, SD = 9.65) relative to AI-assisted participants (M = 70.25, SD = 10.82), p < .001. Immediate knowledge retention scores showed comparatively modest differences between the experimental and control groups (82.30% versus 80.10%, respectively). However, delayed retention assessments revealed a substantial performance advantage for the control group (74.60%) over AI-assisted learners (65.20%), indicating greater knowledge deterioration following AI-supported learning. These findings suggest that although GenAI effectively reduces perceived mental effort during academic tasks, such efficiency gains may coincide with diminished analytical engagement and weaker long-term knowledge retention. The study extends cognitive load theory and cognitive offloading perspectives by identifying a potential trade-off between immediate learning efficiency and sustained cognitive development. The findings underscore the importance of pedagogically structured GenAI integration that encourages independent reasoning, active knowledge construction, and meaningful cognitive engagement rather than passive dependence on AI-generated responses. Implications for instructional design, assessment practices, and responsible AI adoption in higher education are discussed.

items.title: Capability atrophy: When AI automation erodes the dynamic capabilities it was meant to build

items.abstract_text: Firms adopt artificial intelligence (AI) automation to strengthen their dynamic capabilities, yet automation can also remove managers from the routines through which those capabilities are renewed. Drawing on the microfoundations of dynamic capabilities, organizational learning theory, and the automation–augmentation paradox, this conceptual paper develops the concept of capability atrophy and specifies when AI automation weakens, rather than builds, firm-level dynamic capabilities. Theory synthesis across research on skill erosion, organizational learning, and human–AI collaboration yields nine propositions, together with a multilevel, multi-wave mixed-methods design that uses behavioral and system-discontinuance measures to test them. The propositions hold that automation intensity relates to dynamic capability change in an inverted-U pattern, turning negative beyond a substitution threshold. Erosion travels through reduced experiential engagement, weaker skill retention, and poorer reliance calibration, and it becomes organizational when tacit knowledge is concentrated and apprenticeship paths close. Retained decision roles, frequent exceptions, and task variety are proposed to raise the threshold, whereas analytics capability alone is not. The paper places capability atrophy within existing skill-erosion research and adds a firm-level, conditional account with explicit falsification criteria. For practice, it implies that managers should track override rates, unaided diagnosis time, and other observable indicators of capability retention alongside the returns on AI investment.

This article argues that when the volume of AI-generated information exceeds users’ processing capacity governed by working memory constraints, attentional resources, and verification capabilities, it produces cognitive disutility rather than enhancement. We introduced a formal model to quantify this interaction, demonstrating that net cognitive benefits decline systematically as information overload increases beyond individual processing thresholds. The analysis reveals that successful cognitive extension depends not on maximizing informational output but on strategically aligning AI design with human cognitive ergonomics and individual differences in processing capacity. Ultimately, truly augmentative systems must minimize cognitive overhead to prevent overload, while preserving users' epistemic agency and decision-making autonomy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Sustained cognitive engagement, short and mistimed sleep, chronic stress and reduced recovery co-occur in AI-intensive environments, yet how this profile acts on brain energy metabolism is unknown. We built a neuron–astrocyte genome-scale model of human grey matter from Human-GEM v2.1.1, contextualised each cell with human single-nucleus expression, made transport, sodium-pumping and glutathione-recycling costs explicit, and calibrated one parameter to measured cerebral glucose use. Without further fitting the model reproduced the astrocytic share of oxidative metabolism measured by ¹³C spectroscopy (15.7% vs 14%), both the oxidative and the glycolytic regimes of human brain activation, and an independent reconstruction; deletion of genes causing inherited brain-energy disorders compromised its energetic margin far more often than deletion of other genes (odds ratio 79, p = 6 × 10⁻²⁰). Translating the five stressors into constraints, sleep loss and cognitive load each exhausted the margin within the protocol range, at a 25% loss of mitochondrial capacity and a 39% rise in signalling demand, whereas circadian misalignment, chronic stress and reduced recovery acted on arms with reserve. Combined, the stressors exhausted the margin at 0.72 times the moderate profile; across 400 parameter draws demand was met in 99.2% at low and 28.5% at moderate exposure. Substrate oxidation, not substrate supply, set the margin: restoring sleep or reducing load restored it, whereas ketone bodies, lactate or fibre-derived acetate helped only when glucose delivery itself was limiting. Results held across thresholds, releases, solvers and enzyme-capacity limits, and the thresholds are testable with ³¹P and ¹³C spectroscopy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Background and Objective. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) solves school math problems on demand. Higher scores during live tool access do not prove retained mathematical competence once that support disappears. Earlier meta-analyses pooled assisted task completion together with unmonitored and closed-book posttests, which obscured whether pupils actually learned to work alone. This PRISMA 2020 systematic review and stratified meta-analysis evaluates K–12 mathematics outcomes by separating test-time resource rules from instructional design. Methods. Two-stream searches across ERIC, APA PsycNet, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, EuropePMC, and bidirectional citation chasing (1 January 2022–8 November 2026) returned 11,061 raw entries and 6,530 unique records. Every sought report was retrieved in full (372 / 372; 0 unretrieved). Eligibility verification and mathematical consistency checks retained 49 K–12 school-mathematics reports across 46 independent cohorts and supplied 36 quantitative contrasts across 20 controlled study families (21 controlled quantitative reports, plus 1 factorial within-AI modality trial synthesized narratively) alongside 28 qualitative, single-arm, observational, and boundary-comparator reports. Random-effects Paule–Mandel and restricted maximum likelihood estimators with classroom cluster adjustments (calibrated intraclass correlation ρ = 0.128) stratified contrasts across Category A (GenAI active during testing), Category B (posttest with undocumented resource rules), Category C (partial human-help restriction), and Category D (explicit closedresource immediate and delayed exams). Results. Within primary multi-cluster and individually randomized trials (k = 14), large concurrent gains during live GenAI access (Category A: g = +0.615, 95% CI [+0.044, +1.185], p = .035) shrank across undocumented posttests (Category B: g = +0.186 [+0.009, +0.362]) and tutor-restricted exit tickets (Category C: g = +0.095 [+0.024, +0.167]) down to a tight null on explicit closed-resource exams (Category D: g = −0.010 [−0.137, +0.117], p = .876; focal contrast Δg = +0.625, p = .036). Extended controlled trials (k = 28) confirmed strong between-category moderation (Q_between = 12.55, p = .0059; Category D: g = −0.035 [−0.149, +0.078]). Pedagogical architecture accounted for all primary post-withdrawal heterogeneity (Q_between = 18.69, p = .0001; I² = 0% within every tier). Unconstrained direct-answer access harmed closed-exam scores (M1: g = −0.205, p = .043), passive hint guardrails blocked harm without yielding net transfer (M2: g = −0.038, p = .173), and architectures enforcing productive cognitive friction (unaided mastery gating, teachable agents, Socratic Pólya scaffolding, and human-in-the-loop oversight) produced durable gains (M3: g = +0.100, p = .0001; extended g = +0.315, p = .0002). Head-to-head within-AI trials (k = 6) favored pedagogical guardrails and teacher mediation over unguarded GenAI (g = +0.645 [+0.215, +1.075], p = .0033), whereas upper-secondary algebra and calculus cohorts showed acute offloading and workingmemory overload. Conclusions. Unstratified, unclustered synthesis inflates verified closed-resource mathematics learning by +0.26 to +0.29 SD (naive g = +0.275 vs. closed-resource g = −0.010). Durable competence requires crossing two distinct thresholds. Instructional systems must block direct answer copying and enforce active learner generation before and after AI withdrawal.

quarantine.abstract_text: Objective This study examined the association between generative artificial intelligence dependence (GenAID) and academic performance (AP) among adolescents, whether attentional control (AC) and physical fitness (PF) mediated this association individually and in sequence, and whether grade level moderated these pathways. Conclusion GenAID directly predicted lower AP and also predicted lower AP indirectly through AC, PF, and AC followed by PF. The findings indicate interrelationships among GenAID, AC, PF, and AP.
